questions.title: How did the Seventh Circuit have appellate jurisdiction after a guilty plea—does 28 U.S.C. § 1291 treat a conditional plea as a final decision?
questions.question_body: The defendant entered a guilty plea but reserved the right to appeal the denial of his suppression motion. The panel proceeds to the merits. Can someone explain the jurisdictional basis here? Is the "final decision" under § 1291 satisfied by a judgment following a Rule 11(a)(2) conditional plea, and are there any limits on the issues the court can hear when the appeal stems from a conditional plea focused on suppression?

questions.title: Does Coleman have Fourth Amendment standing to challenge a search consented to by his spouse, and how do Matlock and Randolph apply when the objecting co-occupant is in another room?
questions.question_body: The opinion says a third party (Lisa) may validly consent to entry (citing Matlock) and that the defendant may challenge the validity of that consent. But what about Georgia v. Randolph, which restricts third-party consent when a physically present co-occupant expressly objects? Coleman was in a back bedroom and never objected at the door. Does being "present" elsewhere in the home trigger Randolph, or does his silence mean Lisa’s consent controls under Fernandez v. California?

questions.title: Did the panel apply the correct standard of review for voluntariness and scope in light of Ornelas v. United States and the bodycam video?
questions.question_body: The court reviews both voluntariness and scope for clear error, while relying on video to "evaporate" factual disputes (citing Scott v. Harris and Norville). Ornelas instructs de novo review of ultimate Fourth Amendment determinations with deference to historical facts. In the Seventh Circuit, is voluntariness purely factual (clear error) but the ultimate reasonableness of scope reviewed de novo, or are both treated as clear-error questions here? How does the existence of bodycam video affect the level of deference to the district court?

questions.title: When does an officer’s phrasing convert a request into a coercive claim of authority under Bumper v. North Carolina?
questions.question_body: The key exchange was the officer saying, "I’m sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure [the kids are okay]," to which Lisa replied, "Okay." Bumper says consent isn’t valid if it’s mere acquiescence to a claim of lawful authority. Why did the court conclude that this "need" language, in context, conveyed a request rather than an assertion of authority? What doctrinal factors make that distinction, and what case law (like Hicks) supports it?

questions.title: How did the court determine the scope of consent during a welfare check, and why did that allow a sweep of multiple rooms?
questions.question_body: The panel applies Florida v. Jimeno’s objective reasonableness test and says the officers could "scan the home, locate everyone, and ask some basic questions" to check on the children’s safety. What in Lisa’s words (e.g., telling them where the kids were, warning about the dogs, and indicating where Coleman might be) objectively authorized movement through multiple rooms? Where is the line between a welfare check within consent and an impermissible broader search absent exigency or a warrant?

questions.title: Is the scope of consent a factual question reviewed for clear error, a legal question reviewed de novo, or mixed—and how does Jimeno fit with Seventh Circuit precedent?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that both voluntariness and scope are reviewed for clear error. But other cases treat the interpretation of consent’s scope as an objective legal question (subject to de novo review) applied to historical facts. In the Seventh Circuit, what is the controlling standard for reviewing scope determinations, and how does the court reconcile that with Jimeno’s "objective reasonableness" formulation?

questions.title: Should the district judge have conducted de novo review of the magistrate judge’s R&R under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1), and does failure to object limit appellate review?
questions.question_body: A magistrate judge recommended denying suppression; the district court adopted the recommendation. Under § 636(b)(1), parties can object and trigger de novo review of specified portions. Did Coleman object below, and if not, would that normally waive or limit appellate review of the underlying issues? How does the Seventh Circuit treat unobjected-to R&Rs in suppression contexts?

questions.title: Why did the panel decline to reach exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery, and when will an appellate court affirm on alternative grounds?
questions.question_body: The government offered exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery as alternative justifications for the entry and sweep, but the panel said its consent holding "eliminate[s] any need" to consider them. As a matter of appellate practice, when will the Seventh Circuit reach alternative grounds to provide guidance or cement the judgment, and is there a doctrinal preference to resolve cases on the narrowest ground (e.g., avoiding separate exigency analysis post-Caniglia)?

questions.title: How does Scott v. Harris affect appellate treatment of video evidence in suppression appeals—can the court rely on the video to override deference?
questions.question_body: The panel quotes Scott that video can "evaporate any factual dispute." In suppression appeals, does the presence of clear bodycam footage license the appellate court to independently assess what happened (functionally de novo on facts) or does it still credit the district court’s view unless clearly erroneous? What are the Seventh Circuit’s limits on using video to displace credibility determinations or inferences?

questions.title: Was a protective sweep under Maryland v. Buie necessary, or is consent alone sufficient to justify the officers’ canvass to locate Coleman and the children?
questions.question_body: Once inside, the officers located occupants and asked questions. The panel frames this as within the scope of consent for a welfare check, not as a Buie protective sweep incident to arrest. Do officers need a Buie justification to move room-to-room if consent was given for a welfare check, or does consent independently authorize that limited canvassing? What doctrinal distinctions matter between a consent-based walk-through and a protective sweep?

questions.title: Are statements from children during a consent-based welfare check admissible to establish probable cause for a warrant, and what if the initial entry were unlawful?
questions.question_body: The children reported a gun and threats, which were used to obtain a search warrant. Assuming the consent entry was valid, those statements support probable cause. But if the entry were unlawful, would the children’s statements be suppressed as fruits, or could doctrines like attenuation or independent source apply, given that the children were identifiable residents? How do courts analyze causation and taint in this scenario?

questions.title: How did Lisa’s initial refusal followed by later consent factor into the voluntariness analysis under the totality test?
questions.question_body: Lisa first said "I’d prefer you not" when asked to enter, later said "Okay" after the officer’s "we almost need to come inside" comment, and then facilitated entry (moving dogs, directing officers). Does an initial refusal usually cut against voluntariness (suggesting pressure overcame resistance) or support it (showing she knew she could refuse and then freely changed her mind)? How do courts weigh repeated requests and brief delays in this context?

questions.title: What role, if any, does Caniglia v. Strom’s limitation on the community caretaking doctrine play, and why did the panel avoid that path?
questions.question_body: This looks like a domestic disturbance/welfare-check scenario where the government sometimes invokes "community caretaking." After Caniglia limited that doctrine in homes, the panel here rests exclusively on consent and explicitly declines to reach exigent circumstances. Is the avoidance of caretaking analysis a deliberate post-Caniglia strategy, and would the facts here have met any recognized exigency standard if consent were lacking?

questions.title: What exactly must a Rule 11(a)(2) conditional plea specify to preserve a suppression issue on appeal, and what issues are then waived?
questions.question_body: The court says Coleman pled guilty while reserving the right to challenge the suppression ruling. Under Rule 11(a)(2), does the written reservation need to identify the specific suppression grounds (e.g., voluntariness vs. scope), or is a general "denial of motion to suppress" sufficient? Which other issues (like challenges to elements of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1)) are waived by such a plea?

questions.title: Does the objective reasonableness test for scope allow officers to infer consent to speak with the children and conduct a pat-down of Coleman, or was separate consent needed?
questions.question_body: Inside the home, officers talked to the children about what happened and conducted a protective pat-down of Coleman (which he reportedly permitted). Under Jimeno’s objective test, does consent to "come in to make sure the kids are okay" include interviewing the children and briefly patting down the allegedly threatening spouse, or would those steps require separate consent or a different doctrine (like officer safety) to be valid?
